title: How the U.S. Destroyed Iran's Entire Navy in 42 Days  The Full Operation
fullText: On February 28th at 1:15 in the morning Eastern time, a Tomahawk cruise missile launched from an American destroyer in the Gulf of Oman. Then another, then another. Within 90 seconds, eight missiles were skimming 50 ft above the water, threading between Iranian coastal radar stations on routes designed to exploit every known gap in coverage. Flight time to the first Iranian naval base on the southern coast, 40 minutes. Nobody in Iran knew they were coming. By the time the sun came up, nine Iranian warships were on fire, sinking, or already sitting on the bottom of the Gulf. By the time the ceasefire was announced 39 days later, the United States had destroyed over 120 Iranian naval vessels, sunk every major warship Iran had ever built, wiped out the entire submarine fleet, burned through more than a thousand fast attack boats, and turned the fourth largest navy in the Middle East into scrap metal scattered across the floor of the Persian Gulf. This is the full story of how that happened. Not the version you got in headlines. The version that shows you every phase, every weapon, every decision, and the one question at the end that nobody in Washington wants to answer. Let us start with what Iran actually had in the water before this war began. Because most people have no idea how large and how layered Iran's naval force really was. Iran did not have one navy. It had two. The first was the regular navy called the Artis. These were the big ships, frig, corvettes, support vessels, and three Russian-built diesel submarines called kiloclass boats. These submarines were so quiet on battery power that Western naval experts called them black holes because once they went silent, finding them was like searching for a specific car in a city with no street lights. The Artesh also operated Iran's flagship, the Jamaran, a domestically built frigot that the regime paraded on state television for a decade. On paper, it carried anti-ship missiles and a surfaceto-air system. In practice, it had never been in a real fight. The Second Navy was the one that actually scared military planners, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy, the IRGC-N. These were not big ships. These were fast attack boats, hundreds [snorts] of them. Small fiberglass and composite holes, most under 15 tons, running at 50 to 70 knots. Some of them reportedly capable of breaking a 100. Each one costing between 50,000 and half a million, and each one carrying an anti-ship missile with a 35 km range. Iran's plan for these boats was called Swarm Doctrine. Send 30 to 50 of them at a single warship simultaneously from every direction. overwhelm the sensors, saturate the defenses. A single interceptor missile fired from an American destroyer costs $5.3 million. The speedboat it is aimed at costs 50,000. That is a ratio of over 100 to1 in Iran's favor. Iran based this entire strategy around a war game that the Pentagon ran in 2002 where a retired Marine general used swarmboats to sink 16 American warships. The Pentagon was so embarrassed they restarted the exercise. Iran watched that simulation and built a navy around it. On top of the boats, Iran had something even cheaper and arguably more dangerous. Mines, between 5 and 6,000 of them, contact mines that explode when a ship touches them. Influence mines that wait for the magnetic signature of a steel hole passing overhead. and rocket propelled rising mines that sit on the bottom, listen for a propeller, and fire a warhead upward at 260 feet per second, punching through the hull from below. In 1988, a single mine that cost $1,500 ripped a 15 ft hole through the USS Samuel B. Roberts, cracked the keel, and wounded 10 sailors. It took 13 months and $89.5 million to repair. A weapon cheaper than a used car nearly sank an American warship. Now multiply that by 6,000. That was what sat along the coastline of Iran on February 27th, 2026. Two navies, hundreds of fast boats, thousands of mines, three submarines, and hidden missile launchers buried inside mountain tunnels. The American military looked at all of it and decided to take it apart in layers. But here is something most people missed entirely about how this started. The United States did not begin by attacking Iran's Navy. It began by making sure Iran's Navy could not see, could not communicate, and could not coordinate. In the first 72 hours, American cyber operations and electronic warfare blinded Iran's radar networks. Tomahawk missiles and stealth aircraft hit command and control centers across the country. The fiber optic cables connecting air defense commanders to their units were destroyed. Iran's internet dropped to 4% of normal capacity. By the end of the first 3 days, Iran's military was trying to coordinate a war using civilian cell phone networks that were already buckling under 10 million people trying to call their families. The people trying to manage the war could not keep up with the war. And that is when the Navy strikes began. The first targets were the big ships, the ones sitting at port. Most people imagine naval battles as ship against ship fights on the open ocean. That is not what happened. Most of Iran's major warships were destroyed while still tied to the dock. They never left port. They never fired a shot. Tomahawk missiles arrived at Iranian naval bases along the southern coast in the early hours of the first morning. The first warhead hit the command building at the IRGC naval base at Bandar Abbas. The fuel storage behind it caught fire. A column of black smoke punched straight up through the morning air. Within minutes, the Jamaran, Iran's flagship, was hit at its home port. The warhead detonated inside the engine space. The ship's back broke at the keel. The stern dropped 4 feet in 30 seconds as flooding cascaded through ruptured sections. Iran's flagship settled into the mud of its own harbor while the crew abandoned through hatches that were already underwater. The ship Iran had put on every poster for a decade was gone in under a minute. Across the Gulf Coast, the same pattern repeated at base after base. Tomahawk missiles hit command posts, radar stations, and fuel storage. Then, fighter jets followed, putting precision bombs through the roofs of hardened shelters, protecting fast attack boats. At one base, a 2,000lb bomb punched through the concrete arch of a boat shelter. The overpressure had nowhere to go. The roof collapsed onto the boats like a fist closing. The boats that were supposed to swarm the straight of Hormuz were crushed under rubble before they ever reached the water. Within 48 hours, the United States had sunk or destroyed 17 major warships and at least one submarine. By March 11th, past 60. By the ceasefire, over 120 vessels destroyed across both navies. Every ship in the Solmani class corvette line was gone. An entire class of warships erased from existence. The converted tanker that Iran used as a floating drone warehouse was burning at its pier. The frig, the patrol ships, the support vessels, all of them either on the bottom or burning so badly that they would never sail again. But while all of this was happening on the surface, something very different was playing out beneath it. Iran's 3 kilocclass submarines were the one asset that genuinely worried American commanders. In the shallow, cluttered waters of the Persian Gulf, where hundreds of commercial ships create a constant wall of noise, finding a quiet diesel submarine is extraordinarily difficult. If even one slipped out and reached the straight of Hormuz, it could lay mines across the shipping lanes or put a torpedo into a tanker carrying 2 million barrels of crude oil. What is publicly known is this. At least one submarine was hit while docked at Bandar Abbas. Another was reportedly tracked and destroyed using a weapon that nobody expected in this role. An ATACMS short-range ballistic missile normally used against land targets was fired at a submarine. The idea sounds absurd until you realize the submarine was sitting in shallow water at a known location. It was not hiding. It was parked. And a weapon that can hit a specific building from hundreds of kilometers away can certainly hit a submarine that is not moving. A third, the Iris Dena, was intercepted by an American submarine in the Indian Ocean south of Sri Lanka and sunk with a single torpedo. Iran's entire submarine fleet was eliminated within the first week. Now, here is where the story shifts because everything I just described was the easy part. Destroying warships tied to docks, hitting submarines that are not moving, bombing shelters full of boats that never launched. The hard part was what came next. Iran's fast attack boats and its mines. Not all of those 1500 small boats were in port when the strikes began. Hundreds were already dispersed along the coastline, hidden in coves, tucked behind fishing villages, or mixed in with commercial traffic. These boats look exactly like civilian fishing vessels on radar. They move fast enough to cross from the Iranian coast to the shipping lanes in minutes. By March 11th, Iran had carried out at least 21 confirmed attacks on commercial ships around the Strait of Hormuz. Some ships were hit by drones from the mainland, others by missiles from fast boats, some by unmanned explosive drone boats modeled on what Ukraine used against Russia in the Black Sea. A Thai cargo ship caught fire after two projectile hits. A Japanese container ship was struck near the Emirates. Two oil tankers were attacked near Bazra, killing at least one crew member. And this is where we need to stop for a moment. The United States destroyed Iran's entire conventional navy. Every major warship, every submarine, billions of dollars turned to scrap in less than 2 weeks. And yet, the Straight of Hormuz stayed closed. Traffic dropped from over 130 ships per day to single digits. Oil prices surged past $120 a barrel. 800 ships sat anchored outside the straight, going nowhere. The most powerful navy in human history had obliterated its opponent and still could not reopen a waterway 21 mi wide. How is that possible? The expensive ships were easy to find and easy to destroy. But the cheap weapons, the fast boats that cost less than a luxury car, the mines that cost less than a motorcycle, those were the ones that actually closed the straight. Iran did not need its navy to blockade the world's most important shipping lane. It needed a few hundred speedboats, a few thousand mines, and the willingness to use them. That was enough to shut down 20% of the world's oil supply. You just heard what the most expensive weapons in the world could not prevent. But something else was being sent to solve the problem those weapons left behind. And it came from a direction nobody expected. The United States realized quickly that carrierbased fighter jets couldn't solve the fast boat problem. An F-18 Super Hornet crosses the shipping lane at over 500 knots. At that speed, distinguishing an armed IRGC boat from a Kuwaiti fishing trwler is impossible. The jets were too fast. The helicopters were too small. The destroyer missiles were too expensive. A $5 million missile aimed at a $50,000 speedboat is not a strategy. It is a math problem that ends in bankruptcy. So, the Pentagon called in an aircraft that the Air Force had been trying to retire for years. A 50-year-old airplane designed to kill Soviet tanks on the planes of Europe. The A10 Thunderbolt, better known as the Wartthog. The A10 is built around a gun, literally. The gun was designed first and the airplane was built around it. a seven barrel cannon that fires 30 millimeter rounds at 3,900 per minute. The cost to destroy a fast boat with this gun is under $10,000. That is a 500 to1 cost advantage over a destroyer's missile. The A10 flies at 300 knots, slow enough for the pilot to see what is on the surface, identify a threat, and put rounds on target. It carries enough fuel to patrol for over 2 hours. It has a titanium bathtub protecting the cockpit that can absorb direct hits from heavy machine gun rounds. It is by every measure the wrong airplane for the 21st century and the perfect airplane for a shipping lane full of speedboats. Around March 19th, a 10 Warthogs began flying patrols alongside Army AH64 Apache helicopters operating from floating forward bases. For the first time in this war, three branches of the American military were operating over a single six-mile corridor. The A10 flew at 3,000 ft, hunting fast boats. The Apaches flew at 200 ft, picking off targets that slipped through. Navy destroyers maintained the air defense umbrella above both. The combination flipped the cost equation entirely. Before this, the Navy was spending millions per engagement against boats that cost thousands. After combined arms arrived, each engagement cost a fraction of what it had before, and the fast boat started dying faster than Iran could replace them. And then came the piece that changed everything. On March 14th, satellite trackers detected the USS Tripoli moving at high speed through the South China Sea. An amphibious assault ship carrying up to 20 F-35 stealth fighters and 2500 Marines. The AAA was a ship most analysts had written off as a failed experiment. The Navy had removed its landing craft capability, but what it gained was a doubled aircraft hanger and the ability to operate 20 stealth fighters from a single deck, a pocket aircraft carrier that cost 3.5 billion instead of 13 billion. The ship they called a mistake turned out to be the answer. For 40 years, Iran built its entire coastal defense around one scenario. American warships approaching from the sea. Mines in the water, cruise missiles from shore, fast boats in the shallows. The carriers already in the region, the Lincoln and the Ford, were too valuable to risk inside what naval planners openly called the bathtub. A 100,000 tons of irreplaceable steel sitting inside a body of water that Iran had spent four decades turning into a trap. But the triple E was expendable enough to get close and powerful enough to matter. Its F-35s could patrol with response times in minutes instead of hours. And its Marines could go ashore, not to invade, but to land on the small islands inside the strait that Iran was using as launch points and shut them down. Iran built defenses against ships, aircraft, and landing craft. The Tripoli had no landing craft. Its Marines came from the sky in helicopters that flew over the minefields. Iran had spent 40 years solving for one variable. The Marines added a variable Iran never built defenses against. Now, I want you to think about something because this is where it gets uncomfortable. The United States spent 39 days and over $200 billion dismantling Iran's military. every major warship, every submarine, more than 120 naval vessels, thousands of land targets, air defense networks, missile factories, command centers, and the largest prochemical complex in the country. By every traditional measure, the campaign was devastating. And yet, on the day the ceasefire was announced, the straight of Hormuz was still effectively closed. 800 ships were still stuck. The oil that was supposed to flow freely was barely trickling. Here's the question I want you to sit with. You just watched the most powerful military on Earth dismantle an entire navy in 39 days. And you saw that despite all of it, a country that spent a fraction of what America spent managed to hold the global economy hostage for over a month using weapons that cost less than most family cars. The ceasefire is here, but 800 ships are still waiting. And the mines on the seafloor are still sitting there. So the question is this. Did the United States prove that its military power can solve any problem on Earth? Or did Iran prove that the right cheap weapons in the right narrow waterway can hold off even the most expensive military ever built? Write your answer in the comments because the people who say military power and the people who say cheap weapons are about to have the most important argument under this video. And if you have not seen our video on how one $1,500 mine nearly sank an American warship and why clearing those mines is the hardest problem the Navy still faces, make sure to watch that one Next.
